name: Muscles of the hip and lower limb (right)
description: Right gluteal, thigh and leg muscles, with the pelvis and lower-limb bones for context.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Muscles of the lower limb
groups.tip: Each thigh section has its own nerve: femoral in front, obturator inside, sciatic behind. Say Grace before Tea names three tendons below the inner knee.

groups.label: Bones (context)
groups.tip: Muscles pull on bones. The origin is usually the steadier end nearer your trunk, and the insertion is the end that moves.

groups.label: Gluteal region and hip
groups.tip: Gluteus maximus pushes your hip back, while medius and minimus keep your pelvis level on one leg. Play Golf Or Go Out Quickly names the six deep rotators, top to bottom.

groups.label: Thigh: anterior compartment
groups.tip: The quadriceps has four heads that share one tendon over the kneecap, all run by the femoral nerve. Iliacus and psoas join as iliopsoas, your strongest hip lifter.

groups.label: Thigh: medial (adductor) compartment
groups.tip: The adductors pull your thigh inwards, like squeezing a ball between your knees. Most use the obturator nerve, but pectineus and part of adductor magnus are exceptions.

groups.label: Thigh: posterior compartment (hamstrings)
groups.tip: The hamstrings start at your sitting bone and cross hip and knee, so they swing your leg back and bend your knee. Semitendinosus sits on Top of semimembranosus.

groups.label: Leg muscles
groups.tip: The front of the leg lifts your foot, the outer side turns it out, and the back points it down. Behind the inner ankle, think Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry.

names.preferred: Bones of the pelvis and lower limb
synonyms: Hip bone, femur, patella, tibia and fibula

content.pronunciation: bohnz of the PEL-vis and LOH-er lim
content.origin: Pelvis is Latin for basin, and limb comes from an old English word for a part of the body.
content.location: This pale frame is the right hip bone, the base of the spine, and the bones of the thigh and leg. It shows where the muscles attach.
content.description: It shows the hip bone, thigh bone, kneecap, and the two leg bones, the tibia and fibula. Muscles grip bumps like the sitting bone and the hip crest.
content.function: The bones are the levers. Muscles pull on them to move your hip, knee and ankle with every step.
content.mnemonic: Sit on your hands and feel your sitting bones. That is where the hamstrings start.
content.clinical: A strong muscle can yank a chip of bone off where it attaches. This happens in young athletes, for example at the front of the hip after a hard kick.
content.hint: The framework of hip, thigh and leg that every muscle here attaches to.

content.origin: From the Greek word for buttock and the Latin for largest. It is the biggest buttock muscle.
content.location: It forms most of the rounded buttock, behind the hip joint. It covers the smaller buttock muscles underneath.
content.description: The largest buttock muscle and the one nearest the surface. It is thick and square, with coarse fibres running down and out.
content.function: It straightens your hip and turns it outward, powering you up stairs and out of a chair. The inferior gluteal nerve powers it.
content.mnemonic: Maximus means maximum effort. You need it for running, climbing and standing up from a chair.
content.clinical: Injections go in the upper outer part of the buttock. This avoids the sciatic nerve, which runs under the lower part of this muscle.
content.hint: The big surface buttock muscle you use to stand up from a squat.

questions.text: What is the main job of gluteus maximus?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the main hip straightener. It drives you up stairs and out of a chair.

questions.text: Which nerve powers gluteus maximus?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve powers gluteus maximus, and this is the only muscle it supplies.

content.origin: From the Greek word for buttock and the Latin for middle. It is the middle-sized buttock muscle.
content.location: It sits on the outer side of the hip bone, above the hip joint. Put your hand on the side of your hip, just below the crest, to feel it.
content.description: A thick fan whose fibres gather from the hip bone onto the big bump at the top of the thigh bone, the greater trochanter.
content.function: It swings your leg out to the side and turns it inward. Most of all, it keeps your pelvis level when you stand on one leg, so every step stays steady.
content.mnemonic: Medius keeps your pelvis in the middle, nice and level, as you walk.
content.clinical: If it is weak, or its superior gluteal nerve is hurt, the other side of the pelvis drops when you stand on one leg. This is the Trendelenburg sign.
content.hint: The fan-shaped muscle on the outer hip that stops your pelvis dropping as you walk.

questions.text: Standing on one leg, the other side of the pelvis drops. Which muscle is weak?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius, helped by gluteus minimus, holds the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.

questions.text: Which way does gluteus medius mainly move the hip?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius swings the thigh out to the side and turns it inward.

content.origin: From the Greek word for buttock and the Latin for smallest. It is the smallest buttock muscle.
content.location: It is the deepest of the three buttock muscles, lying right under gluteus medius on the outer hip bone.
content.description: A thin fan that gathers onto the front of the big bump at the top of the thigh bone.
content.function: It swings your leg out to the side and turns it inward. With gluteus medius, it keeps your pelvis level as you walk.
content.mnemonic: Minimus is the smallest and the deepest, sitting at minimum distance from the bone.
content.clinical: Tears in its tendon and the gluteus medius tendon are a common cause of pain on the outer side of the hip.
content.hint: The smallest, deepest buttock muscle, lying right on the hip bone under the middle one.

questions.text: Which is the deepest of the three buttock muscles?
questions.explanation: Gluteus minimus lies under gluteus medius, right on the hip bone.

content.origin: From the Latin for tightener of the broad band. It pulls on a long strap down your thigh.
content.location: It sits at the front and side of the hip, just below and behind the bony point at the front of the pelvis.
content.description: A short flat muscle that runs into the iliotibial tract, a long tough band down the outside of the thigh.
content.function: It tightens the band down your outer thigh to steady your hip and knee. It also helps lift the thigh forward and out to the side.
content.mnemonic: TFL stands for Tightens Fascia Lata, the broad band of the thigh.
content.clinical: If the band is tight, it rubs on the outside of the knee. Runners and cyclists feel this as iliotibial band syndrome.
content.hint: The small muscle at the front edge of the hip that tightens the long band down the outside of the thigh.

questions.text: Tensor fasciae latae pulls on which structure?
questions.explanation: Tensor fasciae latae runs into the iliotibial tract, the tough band down the outside of the thigh.

content.origin: From the Latin for pear-shaped.
content.location: It lies deep in the buttock. It runs from the front of the sacrum, out through a gap in the pelvis, to the top of the thigh bone.
content.description: A flat, pear-shaped muscle. It is the key landmark of the buttock, because the sciatic nerve usually comes out just below it.
content.function: It turns your thigh outward, like when you point your toes out. It also helps hold the ball of the hip in its socket.
content.mnemonic: Picture a pear stuck in a doorway. Nerves and vessels squeeze past above and below it.
content.clinical: A tight piriformis can press on the sciatic nerve. This causes buttock pain that can run down the leg, like sciatica.
content.hint: The pear-shaped deep buttock muscle from the sacrum, with the body's biggest nerve appearing just below it.

questions.text: Which nerve usually comes out just below piriformis and can be irritated by it?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve normally leaves the pelvis just below piriformis, so a tight muscle can press on it.

questions.text: Piriformis mainly turns the straight hip which way?
questions.explanation: Piriformis turns the straight hip outward, so your toes point out.

content.origin: From the Latin for to block up, because it covers a hole in the hip bone, and internus, meaning inner.
content.location: It starts inside the pelvis on the side wall. Then it turns a sharp corner round the back of the hip bone to reach the top of the thigh bone.
content.description: A fan-shaped muscle whose tendon bends almost at a right angle, like a rope over a pulley. Two tiny muscles, the gemelli, run alongside it.
content.function: It turns your thigh outward and keeps the ball of the hip steady in its socket.
content.mnemonic: Internus starts inside. It begins within the pelvis, then slips out through the lesser sciatic gap.
content.clinical: It forms part of the pelvic side wall. In some pelvic floor problems it can cause deep pelvic or hip pain.
content.hint: The muscle that starts inside the pelvis on its side wall and bends round a notch to reach the thigh bone.

questions.text: Where does obturator internus start?
options: Outer surface of the hip bone
Inside the pelvis, on the membrane over a hole
questions.explanation: Obturator internus starts inside the pelvis, on the membrane covering the obturator hole and the bone around it.

content.origin: From the Latin for square, and femoris, meaning of the thigh.
content.location: It lies deep in the lower buttock. It runs straight across from the sitting bone to the back of the upper thigh bone.
content.description: A short, flat, rectangular muscle. It is the lowest of the deep hip turners.
content.function: It turns your thigh outward and helps hold the ball of the hip in its socket.
content.mnemonic: Quadratus means square. It is the square block at the bottom of the stack of hip turners.
content.clinical: If the gap between the sitting bone and the thigh bone narrows, this muscle gets pinched. This causes deep buttock pain.
content.hint: The square, flat muscle at the bottom of the deep hip turners, from the sitting bone to the thigh bone.

questions.text: What is quadratus femoris named for?
questions.explanation: Quadratus means square, and this muscle is a flat rectangle.

content.origin: Named after the ilium, the wide upper part of the hip bone.
content.location: It lines the inside of the bowl of your hip bone. Then it passes under the groin crease to the front of the hip.
content.description: A fan-shaped muscle that joins the psoas tendon. Together they are called iliopsoas.
content.function: With psoas major, it lifts your thigh forward, like marching or climbing a step. The femoral nerve powers it.
content.mnemonic: Iliacus and psoas together make iliopsoas. Think: I lift my leg.
content.clinical: Bleeding into this muscle, for example in people on blood thinners, can press on the femoral nerve. The thigh then gets weak and numb.
content.hint: The muscle filling the inner bowl of the hip bone that joins the lower back muscle to reach the thigh bone.

questions.text: Iliacus joins which muscle to form iliopsoas?
questions.explanation: Iliacus and psoas major share one tendon on the thigh bone, so together they are called iliopsoas.

content.origin: From the Greek word for loin muscle. In a cow, it is the tenderloin steak.
content.location: It runs beside your lower spine, deep inside the belly. It passes down over the rim of the pelvis and under the groin to the thigh bone.
content.description: A long, thick, spindle-shaped muscle. It is the only muscle that joins your spine directly to your leg.
content.function: It lifts your thigh forward, like marching up stairs. It also helps you bend forward and sideways at the waist.
content.mnemonic: Think of the tenderloin steak. It runs along the lower back, right beside the spine.
content.clinical: If something inflamed lies against it, such as an appendix or an abscess, stretching the hip back hurts. This is called the psoas sign.
content.hint: The long loin muscle that runs from the lower spine to the inner upper thigh bone.

questions.text: Where does psoas major start?
questions.explanation: Psoas major starts on the lowest back vertebrae, from T12 to L5, then runs down to the thigh bone.

questions.text: Pain when the hip is pulled backward, the psoas sign, can point to inflammation near which muscle?
questions.explanation: Stretching psoas major pulls on whatever inflamed thing lies beside it, so the stretch hurts.

content.origin: From the Latin for tailor. Tailors once sat cross-legged, the very position this muscle helps make.
content.location: It crosses the front of the thigh at a slant, from the bony point at the front of the pelvis to the inner side of the knee.
content.description: The longest muscle in the body, a narrow strap. It forms the outer edge of the femoral triangle in the groin.
content.function: It helps lift, open and turn out your hip and bend your knee. Together that puts you in the cross-legged position.
content.mnemonic: Three tendons meet below the inner knee. Say Grace before Tea: Sartorius, Gracilis and semiTendinosus, with sartorius in front.
content.clinical: The fluid sac under these three tendons can get inflamed. This causes pain on the upper inner shin, common in runners and people with knee arthritis.
content.hint: The longest strap muscle in the body, crossing the thigh at a slant from the front of the pelvis to the inner knee.

questions.text: Sartorius is named after which job?
questions.explanation: Sartor is Latin for tailor. Tailors sat cross-legged, and this muscle helps you sit that way.

questions.text: Which three tendons meet at the pes anserinus below the inner knee?
questions.explanation: Say Grace before Tea: Sartorius, Gracilis and semiTendinosus all meet on the upper inner shin.

content.origin: From the Latin for straight, and femoris, meaning of the thigh. It runs straight down the thigh.
content.location: It runs straight down the middle of the front of the thigh. It sits on top of vastus intermedius, between the other two vasti.
content.description: A spindle-shaped muscle with feather-like fibres. It is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip as well as the knee.
content.function: It straightens your knee and lifts your thigh forward at the same time, which is exactly what you do when you kick a ball.
content.mnemonic: Rectus runs straight down the middle and crosses two joints. Think of kicking a ball.
content.clinical: In teenagers, a hard kick can pull its starting point off the front of the pelvis, taking a chip of bone with it.
content.hint: The straight central muscle of the front thigh group, the only one that also crosses the hip.

questions.text: Which quadriceps muscle also lifts the thigh at the hip?
questions.explanation: Rectus femoris starts on the pelvis, so it crosses the hip and lifts the thigh as well as straightening the knee.

content.origin: From the Latin for huge, and lateralis, meaning on the side.
content.location: It runs down the outer side of your thigh, under the tough iliotibial band.
content.description: The biggest of the four quadriceps muscles, broad and thick.
content.function: It straightens your knee, like standing up from a chair or kicking a ball. The femoral nerve powers it.
content.mnemonic: Lateral is largest. It is the big muscle on the outside of your thigh.
content.clinical: It is a common spot for injections, especially in babies, in the middle third of the outer front thigh.
content.hint: The biggest front thigh muscle, on the outer side under the long band, a common injection site in babies.

questions.text: Which thigh muscle is a common injection site in babies?
questions.explanation: The outer front thigh over vastus lateralis is safe and well developed in babies, so it is a favourite injection site.

content.origin: From the Latin for huge, and medialis, meaning toward the middle.
content.location: It is on the inner side of the front of your thigh. It makes the teardrop bulge just above and inside the kneecap.
content.description: A large quadriceps muscle. Its lowest fibres slant across and pull the kneecap inward.
content.function: It straightens your knee. Its lower fibres keep your kneecap running straight in its groove, like a guide rail.
content.mnemonic: Medialis makes the teardrop on the inside of the knee.
content.clinical: Weak lower fibres are linked to the kneecap running off track and pain at the front of the knee. This part shrinks quickly after a knee injury.
content.hint: The teardrop bulge of the front thigh group, just above and inside the kneecap.

questions.text: The teardrop bulge above and inside the kneecap is made by which muscle?
questions.explanation: The low slanting fibres of vastus medialis form the teardrop just above the inner kneecap.

content.origin: From the Latin for huge, and intermedius, meaning in between.
content.location: It is the deepest quadriceps muscle. It lies right on the front and outer side of the thigh bone, under rectus femoris.
content.description: A broad muscle wrapped round the thigh bone, hidden between the other vasti.
content.function: It straightens your knee, helping you rise from a squat or climb stairs.
content.mnemonic: Intermedius is in the middle and underneath. You cannot see it without lifting rectus femoris.
content.clinical: A knee to the front of the thigh can crush it against the bone, giving a painful dead leg. Sometimes bone even forms in the muscle.
content.hint: The deepest front thigh muscle, lying right on the thigh bone under the straight central one.

questions.text: Which quadriceps muscle lies under rectus femoris, right on the thigh bone?
questions.explanation: Vastus intermedius lies on the front and outer thigh bone, hidden under rectus femoris.

content.origin: From the Latin for comb. It starts on a comb-like ridge of the pubic bone.
content.location: It sits at the top of the inner thigh, in the floor of the groin triangle, between iliopsoas and adductor longus.
content.description: A flat, square muscle. It is the highest of the inner thigh group.
content.function: It pulls your thigh in and helps lift it forward, like crossing your legs. It is usually powered by the femoral nerve.
content.mnemonic: Pectineus is the comb at the top of the inner thigh. It has two jobs and sometimes two nerves.
content.clinical: It can be strained along with the other inner thigh muscles in a groin injury.
content.hint: The flat square muscle in the floor of the groin triangle, the highest of the inner thigh group.

questions.text: Unlike most inner thigh muscles, pectineus is usually powered by which nerve?
questions.explanation: Pectineus usually runs on the femoral nerve, sometimes with help from the obturator nerve that powers the other adductors.

content.origin: From the Latin for to bring toward, and longus, meaning long. It brings your leg toward the middle.
content.location: It lies in the upper inner thigh, the front-most of the inner thigh muscles. It forms the inner edge of the groin triangle.
content.description: A large fan-shaped muscle. Its strong tendon stands out in your groin when you squeeze your knees together.
content.function: It pulls your thigh in toward the other leg, like squeezing a ball between your knees. It also helps lift the thigh.
content.mnemonic: The groin triangle has three borders, SAIL: Sartorius, Adductor Longus and the Inguinal Ligament.
content.clinical: It is the inner thigh muscle most often strained in a groin injury. This is common in football, hockey and other sports with kicks and quick turns.
content.hint: The front-most inner thigh muscle, whose tendon stands out in the groin and edges the groin triangle.

questions.text: Which muscle is most often hurt in a groin strain?
questions.explanation: Adductor longus is the inner thigh muscle most often strained, especially in kicking and turning sports.

questions.text: Adductor longus forms the inner edge of which area?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle in the groin is edged by sartorius, adductor longus and the inguinal ligament.

content.origin: From the Latin for to bring toward, and brevis, meaning short.
content.location: It lies in the upper inner thigh, under pectineus and adductor longus, and in front of adductor magnus.
content.description: A short triangular muscle. The obturator nerve splits into two branches, one in front of it and one behind.
content.function: It pulls your thigh in toward the other leg and helps lift it forward.
content.mnemonic: Brevis is brief and sandwiched, with longus in front and magnus behind.
content.clinical: It can be hurt along with adductor longus in a groin strain.
content.hint: The short triangular inner thigh muscle sandwiched between the long and large ones, with nerve branches on each face.

questions.text: Adductor brevis is sandwiched between which two muscles?
options: Adductor longus in front and adductor magnus behind
questions.explanation: Adductor brevis sits between adductor longus in front and adductor magnus behind, like the filling in a sandwich.

content.origin: From the Latin for to bring toward, and magnus, meaning great.
content.location: It is the deepest and most rear of the inner thigh muscles. It fills much of the inner and back part of the thigh.
content.description: A huge triangle with two parts. A gap near its lower end, the adductor hiatus, lets the main thigh vessels pass to the back of the knee.
content.function: It pulls your thigh in powerfully. Its front part helps lift the thigh and its hamstring part helps straighten the hip.
content.mnemonic: Magnus has two parts and two nerves. The adductor part uses the obturator nerve, and the hamstring part uses the sciatic nerve.
content.clinical: At the gap in this muscle, the femoral artery becomes the artery behind the knee. This is a common place for it to narrow in artery disease.
content.hint: The largest inner thigh muscle, half adductor and half hamstring, with a gap for the main vessels near the knee.

questions.text: The hamstring part of adductor magnus is powered by which nerve?
options: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve
questions.explanation: The hamstring part starts on the sitting bone and is powered by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve, like the other hamstrings.

questions.text: What is the gap in adductor magnus that lets the thigh vessels reach the back of the knee?
questions.explanation: The femoral vessels pass through the adductor hiatus to reach the hollow behind the knee.

content.origin: From the Latin for slender. It is a long, graceful strap.
content.location: It is the innermost muscle of the inner thigh, right under the skin. It runs from the pubic bone to the upper inner shin.
content.description: A long, thin strap. It is the only inner thigh muscle that crosses the knee.
content.function: It pulls your thigh in, bends your knee and helps turn the leg inward, like gripping a horse with your knees.
content.mnemonic: Gracilis is graceful and slender. It is the G in Say Grace before Tea.
content.clinical: You can manage without it. So its tendon, often with semitendinosus, is a common graft to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament in the knee.
content.hint: The slender surface strap down the inside of the thigh, the only inner thigh muscle that crosses the knee.

questions.text: Which inner thigh muscle also crosses the knee and helps bend it?
questions.explanation: Gracilis attaches to the upper inner shin, so it bends the knee as well as pulling the thigh in.

content.origin: From the Latin for two heads, and femoris, meaning of the thigh. It is the two-headed thigh muscle.
content.location: It is the outer hamstring, on the back and outer side of the thigh. Its tendon forms the upper outer edge of the hollow behind the knee.
content.description: It has a long head from the pelvis and a short head from the thigh bone. They join in one tendon to the top of the fibula.
content.function: It bends your knee and turns the leg outward when the knee is bent. Its long head also straightens the hip as you run.
content.mnemonic: Biceps goes to the fibula. B and F sit together on the outer side.
content.clinical: Hamstring strains are common in sprinting and often hit the long head. The short head does not cross the hip, so it is not a true hamstring.
content.hint: The two-headed outer muscle at the back of the thigh, whose tendon runs to the top of the fibula.

questions.text: Where does biceps femoris attach below the knee?
questions.explanation: Both heads join into one tendon that attaches to the head of the fibula, on the outer side of the knee.

questions.text: Which part of biceps femoris is not a true hamstring, because it does not cross the hip?
questions.explanation: The short head starts on the thigh bone, so it works only the knee. It is also powered by a different nerve, the common fibular nerve.

content.origin: From the Latin for half tendon. Its lower half is a long, cord-like tendon.
content.location: It is an inner hamstring on the back of the thigh, lying on top of semimembranosus.
content.description: A fleshy upper part with a long cord of a tendon below, which curves round the inner knee.
content.function: It straightens your hip and bends your knee, as when you pull your heel back while running. With the knee bent, it turns the leg inward.
content.mnemonic: Semi-Tendinosus sits on Top and has a long Tendon. It is the T in Say Grace before Tea.
content.clinical: Surgeons often take its tendon, sometimes with gracilis, to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament in the knee.
content.hint: The inner hamstring with a long cord-like tendon, lying on top of its flatter partner and joining the three-tendon fan below the knee.

questions.text: Which hamstring lies on top of semimembranosus?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus lies on top of semimembranosus. Feel for its thin cord of a tendon at the back of the inner knee.

questions.text: Semitendinosus does all of these EXCEPT which one?
questions.explanation: Like all hamstrings, it bends the knee. Straightening the knee is the job of the quadriceps at the front.

content.origin: From the Latin for half membrane. Its upper part is a flat, sheet-like tendon.
content.location: It is the deeper inner hamstring, under semitendinosus. It ends on the back of the inner top of the tibia.
content.description: A broad muscle with a flat, sheet-like upper tendon. Lower down, it is bulkier than semitendinosus.
content.function: It straightens your hip and bends your knee, like driving your leg back as you sprint. With the knee bent, it turns the leg inward.
content.mnemonic: Membranosus has a membrane at the top, and it lies under its tendon partner.
content.clinical: A Baker's cyst, a fluid swelling behind the knee, often grows from the sac between this muscle and the inner calf muscle.
content.hint: The deeper inner hamstring with a flat sheet-like upper tendon, ending on the back of the inner top of the tibia.

questions.text: Where does semimembranosus attach below the knee?
options: Back of the inner top of the tibia
Bump on the front of the tibia
Outer knob of the thigh bone
questions.explanation: Semimembranosus attaches to the back of the medial condyle, the inner top of the tibia.

content.origin: From the Latin for shin bone, which once meant flute, and anterior, meaning in front.
content.location: It lies just to the outside of the sharp front edge of your shin bone. Lift your toes and feel it harden.
content.description: A thick surface muscle. Its tendon is the easy one to feel at the inner front of the ankle.
content.function: It lifts your foot so your toes clear the ground as you walk, and it turns the sole inward. It also helps hold up the inner arch.
content.mnemonic: At the front of the ankle, from inside out: Tom Has A Very Nervous Disposition. Tibialis anterior is Tom, the innermost.
content.clinical: If the deep fibular nerve that powers it is hurt, the foot drops and you lift your knee high to walk. Overuse causes shin splints.
content.hint: The main shin muscle beside the front edge of the tibia that lifts your foot and turns the sole inward.

questions.text: Which muscle is the main foot lifter and also turns the sole inward?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior pulls your foot up and turns the sole inward. It is the muscle you feel on your shin.

questions.text: After a common fibular nerve injury, the foot drops. Which muscle has become weak?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior is the main foot lifter. It is powered by the deep fibular nerve, a branch of the common fibular nerve.

content.origin: From the Latin for long straightener of the toes.
content.location: It lies at the front of the leg, on the outer side of tibialis anterior. Its tendons fan out over the top of your foot.
content.description: A feather-like muscle whose tendon splits into four, one for each of the four smaller toes.
content.function: It lifts your four smaller toes and helps pull your foot up, so you do not trip on the kerb.
content.mnemonic: Digitorum means digits, your small toes two to five. Hallucis means hallux, your big toe.
content.clinical: If you cannot lift your toes along with foot drop, it helps pin down an injury to the fibular nerve.
content.hint: The front leg muscle whose four tendons show on top of your foot, going to the small toes when you lift them.

questions.text: Extensor digitorum longus lifts which toes?
questions.explanation: Its four tendons go to toes two to five, so it lifts the four smaller toes.

content.origin: From the Latin for long straightener of the big toe. Hallux means big toe.
content.location: It lies deep at the front of the leg, between tibialis anterior and the long toe straightener. Its tendon comes to the surface at the ankle.
content.description: A thin muscle whose tendon stands out on top of your foot when you lift your big toe.
content.function: It lifts your big toe and helps pull your foot up, so the toe clears the ground as you step.
content.mnemonic: Hallux means big toe. Extensor hallucis lifts the hallux.
content.clinical: Testing how strongly you can lift your big toe is a quick check of the L5 nerve root in your lower back.
content.hint: The tendon that pops up on top of your foot when you lift only your big toe.

questions.text: Weakness lifting the big toe is a useful test of which nerve root?
questions.explanation: Lifting the big toe depends on the L5 nerve root, so weakness points to a problem at that level of the lower back.

content.origin: From the Latin for pin or clasp, and longus, meaning long. Its old name, peroneus, comes from a Greek word with the same meaning.
content.location: It lies on the outer side of the leg, on top of fibularis brevis. Its tendon passes behind the outer ankle bone and under the foot.
content.description: A long muscle with a long tendon. The tendon crosses right under the sole to reach the big toe side of the foot.
content.function: It turns your sole outward, helps point your foot down and braces your arches. The superficial fibular nerve powers it.
content.mnemonic: Longus goes a long way, behind the ankle and under the foot. With tibialis anterior, it forms a stirrup under your arch.
content.clinical: It helps stop you rolling your ankle inward. Its tendon can tear or slip out of place behind the outer ankle bone.
content.hint: The surface outer leg muscle whose long tendon crosses under the sole to the base of the first long foot bone.

questions.text: What is the main job of the fibularis, or peroneus, muscles?
questions.explanation: The outer leg muscles turn the sole outward. This is called eversion, and it helps you recover from a wobble on uneven ground.

questions.text: Which nerve powers fibularis longus?
questions.explanation: The superficial fibular nerve powers the muscles on the outer side of the leg.

content.origin: From the Latin for pin or clasp, and brevis, meaning short. Its old name was peroneus brevis.
content.location: It lies on the outer side of the leg, under fibularis longus. Its tendon runs right behind the outer ankle bone.
content.description: A shorter, lower muscle whose tendon ends on the outer edge of your foot.
content.function: It turns your sole outward and helps point your foot down. It helps steady you when your ankle starts to roll.
content.mnemonic: Brevis is brief and goes to the fifth long foot bone, on the little toe side.
content.clinical: When the ankle rolls inward suddenly, this tendon can pull a chip of bone off the base of the fifth long foot bone.
content.hint: The short outer leg muscle under its longer partner, ending on the base of the fifth long foot bone.

questions.text: Rolling your ankle can pull off the base of the fifth long foot bone. Which muscle does the pulling?
questions.explanation: Fibularis brevis attaches to the base of the fifth metatarsal, so a sudden ankle roll can make it pull a piece of bone away.

content.origin: From the Greek for belly of the leg. It forms the round belly of your calf.
content.location: It is the surface calf muscle at the back of the leg. Its two heads form the lower edges of the hollow behind the knee.
content.description: Two heads, inner and outer, make the calf bulge and join soleus in the Achilles tendon. The tibial nerve powers them.
content.function: It points your foot down and lifts your heel when you walk, run, jump or stand on tiptoe. It works best with the knee straight and also helps bend the knee.
content.mnemonic: Gastrocnemius has two heads and soleus has one. Three heads, one tendon, called triceps surae.
content.clinical: A sudden push-off can tear its inner head, causing a sharp pain in the calf. This is called tennis leg.
content.hint: The two-headed surface calf muscle that crosses the back of the knee and makes the calf bulge.

questions.text: Gastrocnemius works on which two joints?
questions.explanation: It starts on the thigh bone and ends on the heel, so it bends the knee and points the foot down.

questions.text: Which nerve powers gastrocnemius?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve powers all the muscles in the back of the leg, including gastrocnemius.

content.origin: From the Latin for sandal or sole, like the flat fish. It is named for its flat shape.
content.location: It lies under gastrocnemius at the back of the leg. You can see its edges on each side of the lower calf.
content.description: A broad, flat muscle that does not cross the knee. Many veins run inside it.
content.function: It points your foot down whatever your knee is doing. When you stand, it stops you tipping forward.
content.mnemonic: Soleus is sole-shaped, and it keeps you standing on your soles.
content.clinical: Each squeeze pumps blood in your veins back up to the heart. Sitting still for a long time lets blood pool, raising the risk of a clot, called deep vein thrombosis.
content.hint: The flat, sandal-shaped calf muscle under the two-headed one, still working when the knee is bent.

questions.text: Which calf muscle points the foot down but does NOT cross the knee?
questions.explanation: Soleus starts on the tibia and fibula, below the knee, so it works on the ankle only.

questions.text: The pumping action of soleus helps prevent which problem?
questions.explanation: Each squeeze of soleus pushes blood up the veins, so it does not pool and clot.

content.origin: From the Latin for heel. It is also named after Achilles, the Greek hero whose only weak spot was his heel.
content.location: It runs down the back of your ankle, from the lower calf to the back of the heel bone. Pinch it just above your heel.
content.description: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It is made by the tendons of gastrocnemius and soleus joining together.
content.function: It passes the pull of your calf muscles to your heel, so you can rise on tiptoe and push off with each step. Tapping it tests the ankle reflex.
content.mnemonic: Remember Achilles' heel. The hero's weak point is this very tendon.
content.clinical: It often snaps in middle-aged people during a sudden push-off. Then squeezing the calf does not point the foot down, a positive Thompson test.
content.hint: The thick cord at the back of the ankle joining the calf to the heel, tapped for the ankle reflex.

questions.text: In the Thompson test, squeezing the calf does not point the foot down. What has probably torn?
questions.explanation: Squeezing the calf normally tugs the Achilles tendon and points the foot. If nothing moves, the tendon is probably torn.

questions.text: Which muscles form the calcaneal tendon?
questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius and soleus, together called triceps surae, share the calcaneal tendon.

content.origin: From the Latin for the back of the knee, the ham.
content.location: It lies deep in the floor of the hollow behind the knee, just above soleus.
content.description: A thin triangle. Its tendon runs inside the knee joint and attaches near the outer meniscus.
content.function: When your knee is locked straight, it gives a small twist to unlock it so you can start to bend.
content.mnemonic: Popliteus is the key that unlocks the knee.
content.clinical: It can be hurt along with the ligaments at the back and outer side of the knee, causing pain and a wobbly knee.
content.hint: The small triangle in the floor of the back of the knee that unlocks the joint so it can bend.

questions.text: Which muscle unlocks the straight knee so it can start to bend?
questions.explanation: Popliteus gives a small twist between the thigh bone and the tibia that unlocks the straight knee.

content.origin: From the Latin for shin bone, and posterior, meaning behind.
content.location: It is the deepest muscle in the back of the leg, between the tibia and fibula. Its tendon passes behind the inner ankle bone.
content.description: A flat muscle whose tendon spreads out under the foot to many small foot bones.
content.function: It turns your sole inward and helps point your foot down. Most of all, it holds up the inner arch of your foot like a sling.
content.mnemonic: Behind the inner ankle bone, front to back: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Tibialis posterior is Tom, closest to the bone.
content.clinical: When this tendon wears out, the inner arch sinks. It is a leading cause of flat foot that starts in adult life.
content.hint: The deepest back-of-leg muscle, whose tendon hugs the inner ankle bone and holds up the inner arch.

questions.text: Failure of which tendon often causes flat foot in adults?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the main muscle holding up the inner arch. When its tendon fails, the arch sinks.

questions.text: Which tendon lies closest behind the inner ankle bone?
questions.explanation: In Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry, Tom is tibialis posterior, first in line and nearest the inner ankle bone.

content.origin: From the Latin for long bender of the toes.
content.location: It lies deep in the back of the leg on the tibia side. Its tendon passes behind the inner ankle bone into the sole.
content.description: A thin muscle whose tendon splits into four in the sole, one for each smaller toe. It crosses over the big toe bender's tendon.
content.function: It curls your four smaller toes, helping you grip the ground. It also helps point the foot down and support the arches.
content.mnemonic: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Dick, for flexor digitorum, is second behind the inner ankle bone.
content.clinical: Surgeons can move its tendon to replace a worn-out tibialis posterior tendon when repairing a flat foot.
content.hint: The deep calf muscle on the tibia side whose four tendons curl the small toes, running behind the inner ankle bone.

questions.text: Flexor digitorum longus mainly bends which toes?
options: No toes, it only turns the foot in
questions.explanation: Its four tendons attach to the tip bones of toes two to five, so it curls the four smaller toes.

content.origin: From the Latin for long bender of the big toe. Hallux means big toe.
content.location: It lies deep in the back of the leg on the fibula side. Its tendon crosses over to pass behind the inner ankle bone.
content.description: A strong feather-like muscle. Oddly, it starts on the outer side of the leg but serves the big toe on the inner side.
content.function: It bends your big toe to give the final push-off as you walk. It also helps point the foot down and support the inner arch.
content.mnemonic: Harry comes last in Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Flexor hallucis is the rearmost tendon behind the inner ankle bone.
content.clinical: Ballet dancers who dance on their toes often inflame this tendon behind the ankle. This is called dancer's tendinitis.
content.hint: The deep calf muscle from the fibula whose tendon crosses to the inner ankle to bend the big toe for push-off.

questions.text: Flexor hallucis longus starts on which bone?
questions.explanation: It starts on the back of the fibula, then its tendon crosses inward to reach the big toe.

questions.text: Dancer's tendinitis behind the ankle affects the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Pointing the foot again and again in ballet irritates the flexor hallucis longus tendon behind the ankle.
